title: Building a plasterboard arch former for a doorway
subtitle: Cut and fit a curved plasterboard arch soffit in a standard rectangular doorway opening
excerpt: How to cut and fit a plasterboard arch former to convert a rectangular doorway into an arched opening. Covers setting out the arc, cutting the MDF former, bending wet plasterboard over the curve, and jointing.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK drylining trade practice for curved arch formers.

glossaryTerms.definition: The structural timber and plasterboard frame that creates an arched opening in a rectangular doorway. It consists of two curved MDF or timber side pieces that carry a strip of plasterboard bent over the arc to form the soffit (underside) of the arch. The former is non-load-bearing: it fills the rectangular head space between the lintel and the curve.

A thin plasterboard (usually 6 mm) specially manufactured to bend around curves without cracking. It is wetted on the paper face before bending to allow the gypsum core to flex. Also known as flexi-board or Gyproc Flex.

content.text: converts a rectangular doorway into an arched opening without touching the structural lintel. The arch shape fills the rectangular dead space above the door frame, and
bends over the curved timber formers to create the arched soffit.

Measure the width of the doorway opening between the door linings. For a semicircular arch, the radius is half the doorway width; draw the half-circle on a sheet of 12 mm MDF using a pencil tied to a length of string pinned at the centre point. For a shallower segmental arch, reduce the radius and set the rise (height at the crown) to 150 to 250 mm. Cut out two identical arch-shaped former pieces with the jigsaw.
Fix the arch formers to the door lining

Screw one former to each side of the door head. The flat bottom edge of the former sits on top of the door head frame. Use 50 mm screws at 300 mm centres through the flat bottom edge into the door lining, and a cross-piece of 50 x 25 mm timber at the crown to hold the two formers parallel. Check that the two curved faces are flush with the face of the plasterboard on each side of the doorway.
Cut and wet the flexible plasterboard

Cut a strip of 6 mm flexible plasterboard to the width of the door opening and long enough to cover the curved arc (calculate the arc length using the formula: arc = pi x radius x (arc angle / 180); for a semicircle it is roughly 1.57 x the doorway width). Lay the plasterboard face-down and dampen the grey paper backing with a wet sponge. Allow five to ten minutes for the moisture to soften the core. The board will begin to bow slightly; it is now ready to bend.
Fix the plasterboard to the former

With a helper, press the centre of the wet plasterboard strip to the crown of the arch and work outward toward the jambs, screwing with 32 mm drywall screws at 100 mm centres as you go. Work quickly before the board dries and stiffens. If the board resists bending, dampen it further. Once fixed, allow the board to dry overnight before applying jointing compound to the edges and seams.

Apply flexible arch tape (a narrow paper tape designed for arches) to the junction between the arch soffit plasterboard and the face plasterboard on each side of the opening. Bed with jointing compound, allow to dry, and apply a skim coat over the entire arch soffit. Once dry, sand smooth with the sanding block and apply finish plaster or decorate directly with a mist coat.

attrs.cause: Board not wet enough, or bent too quickly in the middle without working out from the centre.
attrs.fix: Dampen the board more generously and work from the crown outward, fixing as you go. Use 6 mm flexi-board only, not standard 9.5 mm board.

attrs.cause: The two former pieces were not identical, or the doorway opening is not square.
attrs.fix: Transfer the arch template accurately to both former pieces from the same template. Check the door head is level before fitting the formers.
